nameStory: The kousa dogwood gets its name from its Japanese origins, where 'kousa' is the traditional Japanese name for this tree. While it's also called Chinese dogwood and Korean dogwood after the other countries where it grows wild, 'kousa' has become the most popular common name among gardeners and nature lovers in North America.
description: Kousa dogwood is a small deciduous tree that grows 26-39 feet tall, originally from East Asia but now commonly planted as an ornamental in New England. It's a member of the dogwood family, closely related to our native flowering dogwood. This graceful tree has a distinctive layered branching pattern and puts on quite a show with showy white flowers in late spring, followed by interesting pink-red fruits that look like little strawberries.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: What look like four large white petals are actually modified leaves called bracts, surrounding tiny greenish flowers clustered in the center. The bracts are pointed at the tips, unlike the notched bracts of flowering dogwood, and appear in late May to June.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves are arranged in opposite pairs along the stems, with smooth edges and prominent curved veins that follow the leaf shape. They feel slightly thick and leathery compared to many other trees, and turn brilliant orange-red in fall.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: The distinctive fruits look like pink-red strawberries dangling from the branches in late summer and fall. They're actually compound fruits made of many small berries fused together, with a bumpy, warty texture that's unmistakable.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Mature bark develops an attractive mottled pattern of tan, brown, and gray patches that peel away in irregular scales, giving the trunk a camouflage-like appearance that's especially noticeable in winter.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: The tree naturally grows with horizontal branching in distinct tiers or layers, creating an elegant pagoda-like silhouette that becomes more pronounced with age.

habitat: In New England, kousa dogwood is primarily found in cultivated settings like parks, gardens, and suburban landscapes where it's been planted as an ornamental tree. It occasionally escapes cultivation and naturalizes in forest edges and disturbed areas, preferring well-drained soils in partial shade to full sun.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge in mid to late spring, followed by the spectacular white bracts in late May to early June, blooming later than native flowering dogwood.
seasonality.summer: The tree is in full leaf with green foliage, and by late summer the distinctive strawberry-like fruits begin developing and ripening to pink-red.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant orange-red colors while the bumpy pink fruits dangle conspicuously from the branches, often persisting after leaves drop.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the distinctive layered growth pattern and mottled, peeling bark becomes the main identifying feature along with any persistent fruits.

funFact: The strawberry-like fruits are actually edible and taste like a cross between a mango and a persimmon, though most people never try them because they look so unusual hanging from a tree!
confusionNotes: Kousa dogwood is most easily confused with native flowering dogwood, but kousa blooms later (June vs. May), has pointed bracts instead of notched ones, and produces the distinctive bumpy strawberry-like fruits instead of clusters of red berries.
contextualKnowledge: Though it's an Asian native, kousa dogwood has become extremely popular in New England because it's more resistant to the anthracnose disease that has devastated many native flowering dogwoods, making it a common replacement in landscaping.
compareHints: Among dogwoods, kousa is unique for its late bloom time, pointed bracts, and strawberry-like fruits. Native flowering dogwood has notched bracts and red berry clusters, while other regional dogwoods like gray dogwood have small white flowers in flat clusters rather than the large showy bracts. The layered branching pattern also distinguishes kousa from shrubby dogwood species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its tree and shrub dogwood relatives, Canadian bunchberry is the only dogwood in New England that grows as a tiny herbaceous perennial on the forest floor.
Among dogwoods, this is the only one in New England with alternate leaves - all others have opposite leaves.
Among New England's dogwoods, red osier is the wetland specialist with the most colorful bark.
Among New England's dogwoods, silky dogwood is unique for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - run your finger underneath any dogwood leaf, and only silky dogwood will feel soft and velvety.
Among New England's dogwoods, flowering dogwood is unique for its large, showy white bracts and tree-like size.

Among New England's dogwoods, gray dogwood is unique for its white berries on red stems - flowering dogwood has red berries, red osier dogwood has white berries on white stems, and silky dogwood has blue berries.
Among New England dogwoods, round-leaved dogwood is unique for its combination of rounded leaf tips and rough leaf texture.

Among New England dogwoods, blue-fruited dogwood is distinguished by its true blue berries - red osier dogwood has white berries, gray dogwood has white berries on red stems, and silky dogwood has blue-white berries.
Unlike our native flowering dogwood with its large white bracts, cornelian cherry has tiny yellow flowers in clusters.
Among New England dogwoods, roughleaf dogwood is unique for its sandpaper-textured leaves - no other dogwood species in our region has this distinctive rough feel.
Common dogwood stands out from other New England dogwoods primarily by its intensely colored winter stems - most of our native dogwoods have gray, brown, or only mildly reddish winter bark.

Among dogwoods, Tatarian dogwood's red stems are most similar to native red osier dogwood, but Tatarian tends to have more orange-red coloring and is found in drier garden settings rather than wetlands.

Korean cornel dogwood differs from most other dogwoods in New England by blooming very early with small yellow flowers rather than white ones, and by producing oval red fruits rather than round blue or white berries.
